nameStory: The canopy jumping spider gets its name from its treetop lifestyle, spending most of its time high up in the forest canopy rather than near the ground like many of its jumping spider cousins. The word 'canopy' comes from the Greek word for mosquito net, which is fitting since these spiders create their own little aerial world among the leaves and branches.
description: The canopy jumping spider is a medium-sized jumping spider that calls the treetops home. Females can grow to about 16mm (roughly 5/8 inch) in body length, making them one of the larger jumping spiders you might encounter. Like all jumping spiders, they have excellent vision and hunt by stalking and pouncing on prey rather than building webs. Their most striking feature is their iridescent chelicerae (the jaw-like mouthparts), which can shimmer with colors ranging from deep purple to brilliant green depending on how the light hits them.

idTips.label: Chelicerae Color
idTips.description: The jaw-like mouthparts (chelicerae) shimmer with iridescent colors that shift from purple to green as you change your viewing angle, like the surface of a soap bubble

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females reach about 16mm in body length (roughly the size of your thumbnail), making them noticeably larger than many other jumping spiders

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, forward-facing front eyes give them an alert, almost curious expression, with the front row of four eyes clearly visible and well-developed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, robust build typical of jumping spiders, with a relatively flat, oval abdomen and sturdy legs built for precise jumping

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Found primarily on tree bark and among leaves rather than on the ground, often seen slowly stalking prey with characteristic jerky movements

habitat: Look for canopy jumping spiders high up on tree trunks, branches, and in the foliage of deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. They prefer the upper stories of the forest, rarely venturing down to ground level. You're most likely to spot them on oak, maple, and other broad-leaved trees where they hunt for insects among the bark crevices and leaf surfaces.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and become active as temperatures warm, often seen sunning themselves on tree bark during mild days. This is when their iridescent chelicerae are most noticeable as they display during mating season.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily spotted hunting in the canopy. Females may be carrying egg sacs or tending to spiderlings during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues through early fall, though they become less active as temperatures drop. Late-season individuals may be seen preparing overwintering sites in bark crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in protected spots under loose bark or in tree hollows, remaining dormant until spring temperatures return.

funFact: Despite being called 'canopy' jumping spiders, they can actually change the color intensity of their iridescent chelicerae like a mood ring - the shimmer becomes more vivid when they're excited or preparing to attack prey, possibly serving as both a warning to rivals and a stunning display for potential mates.
confusionNotes: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, this species is easily confused with the much more common Bold Jumping Spider. Look for the distinctive iridescent purple-green chelicerae - Bold Jumping Spiders have bright metallic green or blue-green chelicerae that don't shift to purple. Remember: 'Purple-green shimmer means canopy dweller.'
contextualKnowledge: This spider is extremely rare in New England, with only 2 confirmed sightings in the region. It's primarily a southeastern species that may be at the very northern edge of its range here, so any sighting would be quite significant and worth documenting with photos.
compareHints: Among the Phidippus jumping spiders, the canopy jumping spider is distinguished by its purple-to-green color-shifting chelicerae, whereas most relatives have consistently colored mouthparts. The Bold Jumping Spider has bright metallic green chelicerae that don't change color, while the Regal Jumping Spider has orange-red chelicerae. The canopy species is also more strictly arboreal than most of its ground-loving cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phidippus relatives in New England, the Bold Jumping Spider has the most striking black-and-white contrast - Grayish Jumping Spiders are more muted gray-brown, while Brilliant Jumping Spiders have more colorful red or orange markings.
